newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-All Blacks' World Cup campaign on a roll.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-All Blacks' World Cup campaign on a roll.

text.p: DUNEDIN, Aug 18 - The All Blacks' 1999 rugby World Cup campaign has been kicked along sooner than coach John Hart had expected, NZPA reports.
Hart was planning to pick up several cup prospects for the tour of Britain in November-December and familiarise them with the All Black and touring environments.
He will still carry out those plans, but players like Carlos Spencer and Taine Randell have given him a flying start.
First five-eighth Spencer, 21, and Randell, 22, have become fully fledged test players a season or two before schedule.
In both cases injuries forced the players into the team.

Spencer replaced Andrew Mehrtens and played in seven consecutive internationals this year and Randell has played in all eight after starting in the first test at No 8 for the concussed Zinzan Brooke. He then moved into Michael Jones' blindside flanker's spot and has been the most consistent forward since.
"That gives me a lot of satisfaction," Hart said.
"We always knew they'd been playing test rugby but they came in and just started straight away, which is very pleasing."
What had been regarded as Spencer's Achilles heels at test level, his goalkicking, he has overcome.
The Aucklander, who grew up in Levin, proved he was just as accomplished as any test rugby goalkicker in the last three internationals, missing just two from 23 attempts.
In fact, both Spencer and Randell have been prominent on the scoreboard.

While Spencer kicked 21 points from five penalties and three conversions for 21 points in Saturday's 36-24 win over the Wallabies at Carisbrook, Randell sparked the points' scoring with the match's first try.
"It was awesome. But I have to thank Zinny (Zinzan Brooke) and Justin Marshall for it," said Randell, who marked his first home test with a superbly executed five-pointer.
Brooke peeled off the back of the scrum and went right before passing to halfback Marshall, who in turn swung the ball back left to allow Randell a clear run to the line.
"We called the same move and Justin scored. He didn't have to pass it back because it was clear for him," Randell said.
The All Blacks scored all their 36 points in the first half then went off the boil completely, allowing the Australians to score all their 24 points in the second half.
Many things were blamed for the All Blacks' scoreless second half ranging from fatigue to easing off because they had 36 points without reply on the board.

The fact remained that while their lead was never threatened for their eighth win from eight tests, including the retention of Bledisloe Cup and the Tri-Series, they allowed Australia to outscore them four-tries to three.
South Africa, in the previous week, scored five tries against them despite the All Blacks' record 55-35 victory.
On Saturday their dressing room resembled a morgue, such was their disappointment, but by yesterday the eight victories had sunk in, Hart said.

Hart and his fellow selectors now begin the task of choosing 36 players for the four-test, eight matches in all, tour of Britain and much attention will be focused on grooming players for the 1999 World Cup hosted by Wales.
His present test team and the reserves, barring injury in the national provincial championships, will be retained for a start.
